definition: Relish means to enjoy something greatly, savoring it with real appreciation.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word relish. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know relish should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The debate captain openly relished the toughest cross-examination questions, leaning into each one like a favorite song.
To like something is mild approval; to relish it is to enjoy it deeply, savoring every part.
To devour something — a book, a meal, a challenge — is even hungrier than relishing it: enjoyment turned into fast, eager consumption.

To savor something is to take it in slowly and attentively, dwelling on every detail — a technique of noticing more than a feeling. To relish it adds hearty delight: real, felt enjoyment on top of the attention. You can savor a broth while merely studying it; you relish it when it makes you happy.

To delight in something is simply to take great pleasure in it — even at a distance, in news you merely heard about. Relishing is closer and slower: you turn the particular thing over and enjoy it in detail. Delight is the pleasure itself; relish is pleasure taken slowly, up close.

When you relax, you literally loosen — the same Latin root laxare, 'to loosen, let go,' whose 'taste left behind' sense gave us relish.
Relish means to enjoy something greatly, savoring it with real appreciation.
Grandpa Miro tells the story of the runaway tractor exactly once per family dinner — never twice, never rushed.
He sets down his fork, waits for the table to quiet, and stretches every pause like taffy, savoring the groans when everyone realizes which story is coming.
He has told it two hundred times, and he relishes telling number two hundred one just as much.
Miro's unhurried pauses and evident savoring of every groan show him wringing full, appreciative enjoyment from the telling — that is what it means to relish something.
warm, versatile; everyday-to-literary

Relish is contained, savoring appreciation — you relish one particular thing, like the irony of a moment or a well-made meal — while revel (also in this unit) throws off all restraint: revelers fill the streets, but a person can relish a sentence in perfect silence.

Every garage has one job nobody wants: the mystery rattle.
Cars come in making a sound no gauge can find, and most mechanics groan when the ticket lands on their bench.
Elena is the exception — she relishes them.
She blocks out the whole afternoon, drives the car herself with the radio off, and works through the chassis bolt by bolt, grinning wider with each wrong guess crossed off.
Coworkers say the slow ones are the jobs she loves most; an easy fix, she complains, is over before the fun starts.
